Delivery pack · August 2026

Watchino

A luxury watch storefront built on Selldone. Sixty-six references, read live from a real shop. It sells nothing — and everything on it is real.

01

The whole shop, in one scroll

A storefront assembled entirely from Selldone data. Not a template with products dropped in — a designed identity, end to end, that happens to read its catalogue from a shop dashboard.

02

Photography as the entry point

The hero is editorial rather than a product plate on a background. The catalogue is reachable from inside the image itself.

Why the markers sit on the strap, not the dial. The first version put them over the watch face — the marker was larger than the subject it pointed at, and hid the thing it was selling.

The card is anchored to its dot, measures its own height, and flips below when there is not room above. Below 768px the markers disappear entirely and the two references appear as ordinary cards; a tap that only reveals a card, needing a second tap to navigate, is worse than two plain cards.

03

A brand narrative without a CMS

A shop can carry a story on the same surface as its catalogue. The salon section is drawn, not photographed — line illustrations of the shopfront, the vitrine and the workbench, because no photography of a fictional boutique exists.

04

Sixty-six references, faceted

Filter by collection, maker, price and availability. The price track is logarithmic: twenty-nine of the sixty-six sit under $19,000 against a $153,889 ceiling, and a linear track buries them in the first eighth.

05

Variants that actually change something

Selecting a finish changes the price, the stock, the SKU and the photograph together. Thirty-seven of the sixty-six references carry variants.

A platform limitation worth knowing

Variants carry a colour hex but no colour name. An accessible label therefore has to be the hex itself or an invented mapping — this project chose the hex, plus a visible “Finish 2 of 5” ordinal, so that colour is never the only indicator. Composite values such as #7B1FA2/#D32F2F are not valid CSS and render as a hard 135° split.

06

Content, accounts, checkout

The parts of a shop that are not the catalogue.

Two notes on honesty

The signed-in screenshot uses a simulated session. OAuth sign-in requires entering a password, which the agent will not do, so a token was injected and the profile call stubbed. The code path is real — the panel reaches the signed-in branch, renders Sign out, and omits the callout. The identity is not.

Order history has never rendered against a real account for the same reason. The request is correctly formed and the empty and error states are honest, but the populated state has not been seen.

07

The same identity at phone width

Not a stripped-down variant. Faceting, variants, price and the buy action all survive within thumb reach.

08

Position

A gallery, not a sales funnel. No countdown timers, no urgency banners, no “X people are viewing this”, no discount popups, no confetti. A reduced price is a struck-through figure in muted grey, on the product page only — never a badge on a card in a grid.

What is live and what is written

This distinction matters more than any screenshot here.

Variants136 rows, with colours, SKUs and images

ReviewsSix, each visibly labelled as a sample
Salon illustrationsDrawn, not photographed
Brand history“Est. 1946” and everything attached to it
Contact detailsAddress, phone, hours
Policy pagesTemplates, each carrying a visible banner
Editorial copyCollection blurbs and section headings

No review, specification, colour name, product detail or API path was invented beyond the labelled samples above. Where real data does not exist, the storefront shows an honest empty state.

10

Seven checks that passed while broken

The most useful thing this project produced is not the storefront.

  1. A contrast audit skipped every element with a background-image ancestor — exactly the elements that were failing.
  2. A dead-control sweep inferred wiring from class names rather than observing it, and reported a working control as dead.
  3. A byte-size check would have passed on the SPA fallback page it existed to catch.
  4. A find-and-replace matched nothing and shipped homepage JavaScript onto four pages, silently.
  5. A screenshot harness captured before hydration and produced empty pages that looked deliberate.
  6. A hero-position check shared its arithmetic bug with the code it was testing, so both agreed and both were wrong.
  7. A colour allowlist written for an earlier catalogue quietly discarded the new one’s real variant data.

Every one was found by looking at the screen.

The rule the project ended with: a check must be proven to fail against a known bad input before its passing means anything. Keep the negative control in the run.
